pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–10 years

- **Topic:** Correlation vs Causation

- **Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically):** Pupils should be taught to report and present findings including causal relationships, to use test results to make predictions and set up further comparative and fair tests, and to identify scientific evidence used to support or refute ideas. Distinguishing 'these two things go together' from 'one causes the other' is what makes a claimed causal relationship trustworthy.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 4/6 Analyzing Data & Constructing Explanations, grades 3–5):** Represent data to reveal patterns that suggest relationships, and construct explanations that establish causal, not merely correlational, links — recognising that correlation does not by itself establish causation is an explicit crosscutting concept (Cause and Effect).

- **Operational details:** The child learns that two things changing together (a correlation) does not prove that one causes the other: there may be a hidden third factor causing both (ice-cream sales and drowning both rise with hot weather), the link may be coincidence, or the causal arrow may run the other way. They practise NOT leaping from 'A and B go together' to 'A causes B', proposing a possible confounder or alternative, and recognising that a controlled/fair test (change A while holding everything else constant) is what can actually establish causation. This is a specific, high-value case of 'could there be another explanation?' and it leans directly on controlling variables.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional). This is a landmark critical-thinking move that guards every causal conclusion. Success = given a correlation, the child resists asserting causation, proposes at least one alternative (confounder, coincidence, or reversed direction), and identifies that a controlled test is needed to establish a true cause.
bestPractices: Use vivid, genuinely spurious correlations (ice-cream sales/drownings, shoe size/reading age) so the trap is felt, then reveal the hidden common cause.
Teach three escape routes from a correlation — hidden common cause, coincidence, or reversed direction — as things to check before claiming cause.
Link causation to the fair test: only holding everything else constant and changing one variable can establish that A causes B.
Have children propose the confounder themselves ('what else could make BOTH go up?') rather than being told it.
Distinguish 'good evidence for a pattern' from 'good evidence for a cause' explicitly when reporting findings.
Frame the correlation/causation check as a special case of 'could there be another explanation?' to connect the habits.
keyRepresentations: Two lines rising and falling together (correlation) with a hidden third variable driving both
The confounder diagram: A ← C → B (common cause) vs A → B (true cause)
Reversed-arrow case (B causes A) and coincidence case
Control-test view: hold the confounder fixed, vary A alone, watch B not follow
Scatter plot whose trend flattens once the confounder is controlled
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that because two things rise and fall together, one must cause the other.
Never considering a hidden third factor that drives both variables.
Ignoring the possibility that the causal arrow runs the other way.
Treating a strong or striking correlation as automatically causal.
Thinking observation of a pattern alone (without a controlled test) can prove causation.
Believing coincidental correlations can't happen in 'real' data.

learn.summary: For ages 8–10, teach that two things changing together (correlation) does not prove one causes the other. Learners practise resisting the causal leap, proposing an alternative explanation (a hidden common cause, coincidence, or reversed causal direction), and recognising that a controlled/fair test — changing one variable while holding everything else constant — is what the curriculum treats as establishing cause. The anchor example is ice-cream sales and drowning (or sunburn) both rising in hot weather, with temperature as the hidden common cause.

activities.title: Bust a fake cause by manipulating a system
feedback: If the learner accepts 'ice cream causes drowning' from the lines moving together: ask what else happens on those days that could push BOTH up — prompt them toward a third factor rather than naming it for them, and if useful sketch the common-cause diagram (temperature → ice cream, temperature → drowning).

When the drowning line stays flat in control mode: 'You held temperature still and changed only ice cream — nothing happened to drowning, so in this model ice cream is not causing drowning. Earlier, when you moved the temperature slider, both lines moved, so temperature is what was driving both.'

In the main ice-cream/drowning scenario (where neither one causes the other), if the learner only debates which of the two caused the other: point out a third option — something outside both could be driving both at once.
In the reversed-direction case, confirm when the learner correctly identifies that B causes A rather than A causing B, and contrast it with the common-cause case where a third factor drives both.
For the coincidence case: note that striking patterns can appear in real data purely by chance, so 'they go together' is only a clue, not proof.
activities.rationale: Manipulating a system and watching a convincing correlation dissolve under a controlled change is intended to make the abstract warning concrete and repeatable; letting the child reveal and vary the confounder themselves is intended to link correlation-vs-causation to the fair-test idea of changing one variable while holding others constant. The confounder reveal, control mode, scatter view, common-cause diagram, reversed-arrow case and coincidence case are optional interaction examples that can make the mechanism visible, not mandatory features.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to report findings including causal relationships and to identify scientific evidence used to support or refute ideas.
NGSS treats Cause and Effect as a crosscutting concept requiring that mere correlation be distinguished from causation, and has students construct explanations establishing causal links (grades 3–5).
learnerActions: Watch two variables — ICE-CREAM SALES and DROWNING ACCIDENTS — plotted side by side as you scrub a month-slider; notice both lines rise together through summer and fall together in winter.
State the tempting but wrong conclusion the data invites ('it looks like ice cream causes drowning').
Reveal a hidden covered slider; find it is TEMPERATURE, then drag it and observe BOTH lines move together because of it.
Switch to CONTROL mode: pin temperature at a fixed value, then raise and lower ice-cream sales on their own, and watch whether the drowning line follows or stays flat.
Optionally switch to a scatter-plot view and watch how holding the hidden factor (temperature) fixed flattens the apparent trend between ice-cream sales and drowning.
Optionally draw or view the common-cause diagram — temperature → ice-cream sales and temperature → drowning — and contrast it with what a true direct cause (ice cream → drowning) would look like.
Explain in your own words why the flat drowning line shows that, in this model, ice cream is not what causes drowning.
Try a reversed-direction case (where B actually causes A) and a pure-coincidence case, and decide which escape route explains each.
activities.intendedInsight: A correlation can be produced by a hidden common cause, a reversed causal direction, or coincidence; holding the hidden factor fixed and changing only one variable is what tests whether a true cause exists.

activities.title: Name the confounder or the test that settles it
feedback: Accepting a claim because the two things 'go up together': redirect to search for a third thing behind both.
When a correct confounder is named: confirm it, then ask what test would hold that factor still while changing only A.
If the learner sorts a coincidental pattern as 'real cause': note that even strong patterns can arise by chance in real data.
activities.rationale: Selection and matching tasks can sharply assess whether a child resists the causal leap and can articulate an alternative; this is a check on the reasoning and does not itself build the manipulate-and-watch-it-dissolve intuition, so it works best after hands-on experience.
learnerActions: For a given vivid correlation (ice cream / drowning, shoe size / reading age), decide whether it shows that A causes B or whether something else could explain the link.
Sort a set of claims into 'correlation only' versus 'evidence of a real cause'.
Match each correlation to its most likely explanation: a hidden common cause, a reversed direction, or coincidence.
For each case, describe a fair test, or explain why one is hard or impossible (for example, you cannot change someone's shoe size), that would help check whether A really causes B.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the causal leap and being able to name a plausible confounder (or the test that would decide) is distinct from merely sensing a claim is wrong.

activities.title: Interrogate a bold causal headline
feedback: For the shoe-size/spelling case: if the learner accepts the causal claim, prompt 'what do older children have more of besides bigger feet?' to surface age as the common cause.

If time order is used as proof ('you eat ice cream then you burn'): give a counterexample where order and cause come apart (a rooster crows before sunrise but does not cause it); separate 'came first' from 'caused'.
Reinforce that a good answer names the hidden factor AND describes a test that isolates the real cause.
activities.rationale: Taking a sceptical questioning stance toward a stated claim models the habit of asking 'could there be another explanation?'. This works best paired with the visual playground, since for this age the reasoning can stay abstract without seeing variables move together and come apart.
learnerActions: Read a bold causal claim (e.g. 'children with bigger feet are better at spelling — so big feet cause good spelling').
Ask probing questions out loud or in writing: Could something else cause both? Which way does the arrow point? Could this be coincidence?
Propose a hidden common cause (e.g. older/bigger children have both larger feet and more spelling practice).
Describe how you would actually test whether ice cream affects sunburn so the weather can't fool you.
State what it would take to convince you that A really causes B, not just goes with it.
activities.intendedInsight: Challenging a causal claim means actively testing it against the three escape routes — common cause, reversed direction, coincidence — and insisting on a controlled test before accepting cause.

constraints: Have children propose the hidden common cause themselves ('what else could make BOTH go up?') rather than being told it.
Teach three escape routes from a correlation — hidden common cause, coincidence, or reversed direction — as things to check before claiming cause.
Explicitly distinguish 'good evidence for a pattern' from 'good evidence for a cause' when reporting findings.
Link causation to the fair test: holding everything else constant and changing one variable is what can establish that A causes B.

Selection, matching and sorting tasks can check whether a child resists the causal leap but do not by themselves build the intuition that comes from intervening and watching a correlation break; use them after hands-on or discussion work.

A tap-to-reveal static diagram can memorably illustrate the trap and the hidden cause, but it does not let the learner intervene to see the link break; treat it as an illustrative scaffold feeding into interactive or discussion work.
Frame this as a special, high-value case of 'could there be another explanation?' and connect it to controlling variables.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source row's NGSS claim is marked verified:false in the original; treat the NGSS citation as unconfirmed and not as evidence that any activity has been tested.

The DfE and NGSS claims are cited as support for the correlation/causation teaching principle, not as efficacy evidence for the manipulation medium; the DfE claim in particular is close to topic-level.

The original framing that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing' and that static art 'can't' forge the understanding are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal claims.

The anchor example appears in two forms across the source (ice-cream/drowning in the learn/recommendation fields; ice-cream/sunburn in the assessment fields). Both share temperature as the common cause; either is usable, but keep the version consistent within a single task to avoid confusing learners.

Feedback that redirects a learner toward a third factor is scoped to the common-cause scenario; in the reversed-direction case, correctly identifying the arrow direction is the intended answer, so the two must not be conflated.

probeDeeper: How could we actually test whether ice cream affects sunburn, so the weather can't fool us?
Here's another: children with bigger feet are better at spelling. Does big feet cause good spelling? What's really going on?
What would it take to convince you that A really does cause B, not just goes with it?
assess.correctAnswer: Strong reasoning rejects the causal claim and identifies a third factor — hot, sunny weather — driving both ice-cream sales and sunburn, so the two rise together without one causing the other. It articulates that things happening together (correlation) does not by itself mean one causes the other, and that you would need to rule out other explanations before claiming cause.

errorPatterns.pattern: Two things happening together means one causes the other ('they go up together, so ice cream causes sunburn').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce the idea of a third thing behind both; ask 'what happens on those days that could cause BOTH?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Endorses the causal claim on the strength of co-occurrence alone.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to search for a third or common variable — considers only 'A causes B' or 'B causes A', never 'C causes both'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the common-cause pattern explicitly with a diagram: weather causes ice cream, weather causes sunburn.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Debates the direction of cause but never proposes a hidden common factor.

errorPatterns.pattern: Post hoc — because sunburn sometimes follows ice cream in time, the earlier one caused the later ('you eat ice cream then you burn, so it did it').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give a counter where order and cause come apart — the rooster crows before sunrise; separate 'came first' from 'caused'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses time order alone as proof of cause.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts the causal claim from co-occurrence, or only argues about which of the two caused the other.
responseLevels.full: Names the hidden common cause (hot weather) driving both, states that correlation alone doesn't establish causation, and can describe a test that isolates the real cause — transferring the pattern to a new example.
responseLevels.partial: Senses the claim is wrong ('that can't be right') but can't name the mechanism — doesn't identify a common cause or how you'd rule it out.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Someone notices that on days when more ice creams are sold, more people get sunburnt. They say 'eating ice cream must cause sunburn.' Do you agree? Explain what you think is really going on.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who conflates correlation with causation accepts 'ice cream causes sunburn' because the two go together. A child who grasps the distinction looks for a common cause. Naming the hidden weather variable is very hard to do while still believing correlation proves cause — so the answer cleanly separates the two groups.
